'''''Skimmia japonica''''', the '''Japanese skimmia''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Rutaceae]]. [[native plant|Native]] to Japan, Taiwan, China, Vietnam, Philippines, and the [[Russian Far East]], it is commonly grown in parks and gardens for its evergreen leaves, fragrant flowers, and attractive fruit. It is a highly [[variable species]], with its [[variety (botany)|varieties]] differing in height, spread, and [[chromosome count]], among other things.

==Description==
''Skimmia japonica'' is a dense, [[evergreen]] shrub.<ref name="missouri"/> The plant grows 60–200 cm tall and is smooth throughout except for the [[flower cluster]]s, which carry a fine fuzz. The branches rise at an angle, are grayish, and bear small glandular bumps called [[tubercle]]s. The leaves are arranged alternately, though they can seem loosely whorled. Each leaf has a short stalk 0.5–1 cm long. The blades are narrow and elongated—6–12 cm long and 2.5–3.5 cm wide—with a tip that narrows abruptly before ending in a rounded point. The base tapers, the margins are smooth, the upper surface is glossy, and the underside is yellowish with scattered oil glands.<ref name="flora">{{cite book |last1=Iwatsuki |first1=Kunio|last2=Boufford |first2=David E. |last3=Ohba |first3=Hideaki|title=Flora of Japan|volume=IIc|pages=43–44 |year=1999 |publisher=Kodansha Ltd. |location=Tokyo}}</ref> Female plants tend to grow wider than male plants.<ref name="missouri"/>

Flower clusters sit at the ends of branches and form small, branching [[cyme (botany)|cymes]] 2–5 cm long and 4–8 cm across. Their stalks are finely fuzzy. The plant flowers in spring. The blossoms are usually four-parted, 5–6 mm across, with tiny triangular [[sepal]]s and [[bract]]s edged with minute hairs. [[Petal]]s are narrow, 4–5 mm long, and dotted with a few clear glands. [[Stamen]]s match the petals in length. The [[style (botany)|style]] is short (0.8 mm), soon falls off, and bears a somewhat rounded [[stigma (botany)|stigma]] divided into four lobes.<ref name="flora"/> The flowers are fragrant.<ref name="missouri">{{cite web | title=Skimmia japonica | url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286767|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org|publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]]| access-date=18 November 2025}}</ref> With the exception of ''S. japonica'' var. ''reevesiana'', the species is [[dioecious]].<ref name="flora"/> The [[vestigial organ]]s of the opposite sex can be prominent, especially in female flowers, the stamens of which may be almost full-sized yet remain whitish and produce no yellow, fertile [[pollen]].<ref name="Taylor"/>

The fruits are spherical [[drupe]]s 6–9 mm wide. Each contains two to five [[Pyrena|stones]], each stone holding a single seed. Seeds include [[endosperm]].<ref name="flora"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
The [[native range]] of ''Skimmia japonica'' includes Japan, Taiwan, and [[Sakhalin]]. In Japan, ''S. japonica'' var. ''japonica'' grows in low-mountain forests on [[Honshu]] (from the [[Kantō region|Kanto]] region westward), [[Shikoku]], and [[Kyushu]], and can be common locally. In Japan, ''S. japonica'' var. ''intermedia'' occurs in the [[southern Kuriles]], [[Hokkaido]], Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. They grow on the [[forest floor|floor]] of [[deciduous forest]]s and are especially widespread in the heavy-snow regions of Hokkaido and Honshu on the [[Sea of Japan]] side. They are much less frequent in the colder, high-elevation deciduous forests of Honshu west of Kanto on the [[Pacific]] side, as well as in Shikoku and Kyushu. Beyond Japan, the variety is also found in the Kuriles and Sakhalin.<ref name="flora"/>

''Skimmia japonica'' var. ''japonica'' and var. ''reevesiana'' range into the [[subtropics]], the latter reaching the Philippines and southern Vietnam; it is also found in the [[Guangdong]] and [[Guangxi]] provinces of [[southern China]] and on [[Mount Omei]] in the [[Sichuan]] province. ''Skimmia japonica'' [[sympatry|shares parts of its range]] with ''[[Skimmia laureola|S. laureola]]'' subsp. ''laureola'' and ''[[Skimmia arborescens]]'' subsp. ''nitida''; it is separated from the former by habitat altitude and possibly [[reproductively isolated]] from the latter by the difference in [[chromosome count]].<ref name="Taylor"/>

==Varieties and cultivars==
''Skimmia japonica'' was the first ''[[Skimmia]]'' species to be [[scientifically described]].<ref name="Taylor">{{cite journal | last=Taylor | first=Nigel P.|author-link=Nigel Taylor | title=A revision of the genus ''Skimmia'' (Rutaceae) | journal=The Kew Magazine | publisher=Wiley | volume=4 | issue=4 | year=1987 | issn=0265-3842 | jstor=45066619 | pages=168–194 | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/45066619 | access-date=19 November 2025}}</ref> Five [[variety (taxonomy)|varieties]] of ''Skimmia japonica'' are recognized: ''S. japonica'' var. ''japonica'', ''S. japonica'' var. ''distincte-venulosa'', ''S. japonica'' var. ''intermedia'', 
''S. japonica'' var. ''lutchuensis'', and ''S. japonica'' var. ''orthoclada''.<ref name="b615">{{cite book | title=植物研究雜誌 | publisher=津村硏究所 | date=1993 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h6bzAAAAMAAJ&q=%2522skimmia+japonica%2522+%2522var.+japonica%2522+%2522var.+distincte-venulosa%2522+%2522var. | language=ja | access-date=17 November 2025 | page=303|volume=68}}</ref> The male and female individuals of ''S. japonica'' were originally thought to represent different species: ''S. fragrantissima'' or ''S. fragrans'' (male) and ''S. oblata'' (female).<ref name="Taylor"/>

The varieties of ''Skimmia japonica'' can be separated by growth habit and leaf size. Plants that spread rather than grow upright, reaching only 0.3–1 m in height and carrying leaves 4–7 cm long and 1.5–2.5 cm wide, belong to var. ''intermedia''. Among these, [[form (botany)|forma]] ''repens'' is distinguished by flat leaves. The plants that grow erect, usually 0.6–2 m tall, and bear larger leaves 7–13 cm long and 2.5–4 cm wide fall into two groups. When the leaves are narrow—ranging from oblong-oblanceolate to narrowly obovate—and measure 2.5–3.5 cm across, the plants represent var. ''japonica'', which extends from the southern Kuriles southward to Kyushu, including [[Yakushima]]. Plants with broader, widely oblanceolate leaves 3–6 cm wide and [[bisexual flower]]s, confined to the [[Ryukyu Islands]], correspond to var. ''lutchuensis''. The fruits of ''S. japonica'' are red except in ''S. japonica'' var. ''intermedia''. f. ''leucocarpa'', which produces white drupes.<ref name="flora"/>

Along with ''[[Skimmia anquetilia]]'', ''S. japonica'' is a likely [[parent species]] of ''[[Skimmia × confusa]]''. Another hybrid, called ''S. foremanii'', was developed in the 1870s by the Scottish nurseryman Foreman, but has apparently not survived beyond a few generations; it was said to be a cross between ''S. japonica'' var. ''japonica'' and ''S. japonica'' var. ''reevesiana'', but this is unlikely because the former is [[diploid]] (2n=30) and the latter [[tetraploid]] (2n=60), which would mean that the resulting hybrid would have been [[triploid]] and thus [[Sterility (physiology)|sterile]].<ref name="Taylor"/>
[[File:Skimmia japonica Rubella.jpg|thumb|The cultivar 'Rubella' has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].]]
The [[cultivars]] 'Fragrans',<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Skimmia japonica'' 'Fragrans' | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/93427/Skimmia-japonica-Fragrans-(m)/Details | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> 'Nymans',<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Skimmia japonica'' 'Nymans' | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/92892/Skimmia-japonica-Nymans-(f)/Details | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> and 'Rubella'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Skimmia japonica'' 'Rubella' | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94155/Skimmia-japonica-Rubella-(m)/Details | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 97 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 11 November 2018}}</ref> Other cultivars include  'Veitchii', 'Oblata', 'Macrophylla', and 'Bronze Knight'.<ref name="Taylor"/>

==Cultivation==
''Skimmia japonica'' is grown in shaded sites for its evergreen leaves, lightly fragrant spring flowers, and the fruit that develop on female plants in autumn. It has no notable pest or disease issues. It is suitable for [[shrub border]]s, [[woodland garden]]s, foundation plantings, [[hedge]]s, and other partly shaded [[understory]] settings. It performs best in moist, [[humus]]-rich, moderately [[fertile soil]]s that drain well, in conditions ranging from partial to full shade. Its leaves can scorch if exposed to full sun.<ref name="missouri"/> ''S. japonica'' was the first member of its genus to be grown in Britain; the earliest record, referring to ''S. japonica'' var. ''reevesiana'', is from [[Kew Garden]] in 1858.<ref name="Taylor"/>
